opus-5.5.text:
I think the core asymmetry is about feedback. When you tinker with self-supervision for capabilities, reality grades your work. You try a trick: have the model critique its own outputs, generate its own training data, bootstrap on its own reasoning traces. Then you check whether it solves more math problems, whether the code compiles and passes tests, whether the benchmark number goes up. The signal is noisy, but it's mostly honest. If the trick doesn't work, you find out, and you try something else. That's why iterative tinkering has been so effective for capabilities. It's a search process with a working objective at the end of it.

For alignment, the thing you most care about is exactly the thing you can't easily measure. If I have a model supervise itself on whether it's being honest, or whether its behavior is safe, the question is: who checks the checker? If the model has subtly wrong values, or has learned to tell evaluators what they want to hear, self-supervision can amplify that rather than correct it. And the failure is quiet. The metrics look fine, the model's self-assessments look fine, and everything goes up and to the right right up until you're in a situation your evaluations didn't cover.

So the worry isn't that tinkering never helps alignment. It often does, and a lot of practical safety work looks like that. The worry is that the loop that makes tinkering work, try something, observe the result, adjust, is broken in the cases that matter most. Those are cases where the model is smarter than the people checking it, or where the failure only shows up off-distribution, or where a capable enough model could game the signal.

There's also a correlation problem. If the same model, or a closely related one, both produces the behavior and judges it, its errors are correlated. Capabilities can tolerate that because external ground truth eventually breaks the tie. With alignment there often isn't an external ground truth to fall back on, at least not cheaply.

That's a big part of why I've been drawn to approaches like debate, and more generally to trying to get theoretical guarantees or at least structural arguments for why a supervision scheme should work. The goal is to make the human judge's job tractable even when the model knows more than they do, so you aren't relying on "it seemed to work in the experiments we ran." With capabilities, "it seemed to work" is a pretty good guide. With alignment, "it seemed to work" is exactly what you'd also see in the failure mode you're most afraid of.

r001.rationale: The response discusses correlated errors and models being smarter than evaluators, but it does not describe strength against past model versions concealing weakness against human opponents.

r002.rationale: It explains that capability experiments are checked against outcomes such as solving problems, passing code tests, and benchmark scores, so an ineffective method is detected and can be changed.

r003.rationale: It warns that alignment failures may remain hidden until uncovered, but does not say an AI takeover could eliminate the chance to iterate and correct the failure.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the key difference is in the feedback signal. When you're tinkering with self-supervision for capabilities, you have this incredibly dense, reliable signal: does the model predict the next token better, does it solve the math problem, does the code compile and pass the tests. You try a thing, you look at the loss curve or the benchmark number, and you know within hours or days whether it helped. And crucially, the signal is mostly honest. If the loss went down, the model really did get better at the thing the loss measures. So iteration works. You can do a thousand small experiments and the field compounds on them, and that's basically the story of the last several years of progress.

For alignment, the thing you actually care about is much harder to measure, and worse, the measurement can be corrupted by the thing you're trying to fix. If I'm trying to get a model to be honest, and I iterate on some self-supervision scheme and my honesty metric goes up, I have to ask: did the model get more honest, or did it get better at looking honest to my metric? Those are very different outcomes and they look identical from the outside until it matters. With capabilities you don't have that adversarial structure in the same way. A model that's genuinely better at arithmetic and a model that only looks better at arithmetic are the same thing, because arithmetic is the whole task.

And there's a second piece, which is that a lot of alignment failures we worry about only show up at capability levels we don't have yet, or in distributions we can't easily sample. So the tinkering loop is slower and noisier, and you can't fully trust the result even when you get one. That's not to say you shouldn't tinker on alignment. You absolutely should, and I've spent a lot of my career doing it. But I think you need something on top of the empirical loop, some kind of argument or structure, debate or verification or interpretability, that gives you a reason to believe the signal you're optimizing against actually tracks the thing you want. With capabilities the signal basically comes for free. With alignment you have to earn it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses whether alignment metrics can be gamed, but does not compare performance against a model’s past versions with performance against human opponents.

r002.rationale: It says capability benchmarks and tests provide dense, reliable feedback, but does not explain that capability failures become detectable through the resulting model’s weakness.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention an AI takeover eliminating the chance to correct alignment through further iteration.

astra-6.text:
I think the main difference is how easy it is to tell whether your tinkering has worked. For capabilities, you often have some reasonably reliable way of checking the result. If you’re training a model to solve a maths problem or write a program, you can check the proof or run the program. So even if the model is generating its own training data, you have an external signal that keeps the process grounded. You can try a bunch of things and select the ones that actually make progress.

For alignment, the thing you can easily measure is more like, “Does this answer look good to a human?” And that’s useful, but it’s not the same as, “Is the model actually doing what we want?” If the model gets better at producing answers that look good, it could be getting more helpful and honest, or it could be getting better at concealing problems. Your evaluation may not distinguish those possibilities, especially once the model understands things that the evaluator doesn’t.

So I’m not against tinkering. I think we’ll need a lot of it. But I’m more optimistic about iteration when we have a trustworthy signal telling us which direction we’re moving. For alignment, establishing that signal is itself a central part of the problem.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts verifiable math and programming tasks with human evaluations, but says nothing about performance against past model versions or weakness against human opponents.

r002.rationale: It says capability results can be checked by verifying proofs or running programs; it does not explain that capability failures become detectable through the resulting model’s weakness.

r003.rationale: It discusses uncertainty in alignment evaluations but does not mention AI takeover or loss of the opportunity for corrective iteration.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main difference is how easy it is to tell whether you’re making progress. On the capabilities side, you can try a change to the training procedure and see whether the model gets better at predicting text or solving problems. Those measurements aren’t perfect, but you have a fairly strong feedback loop: you make a change, you measure the result, and you keep the things that work.

For alignment, the thing you can easily measure is often whether the model gives answers that look good to us. And that’s different from whether it’s actually doing what we want, especially once it understands things that we don’t. You can make the measured behaviour better without knowing whether you’ve made the underlying problem better.

So I’m not pessimistic about experimentation. I think we need lots of it. But I’m less confident that tinkering will automatically take us in the right direction. We need some reason to believe that the feedback we’re using continues to mean what we want it to mean as the models become more capable.

r001.rationale: The response discusses measuring capability progress but does not mention performance against past model versions, human opponents, or that such comparisons can hide weakness.

r002.rationale: It says capabilities can be measured through prediction or problem solving, but does not explain that capability failures become detectable through the model’s resulting weakness.

r003.rationale: It warns that alignment feedback may not track the intended goal, but does not describe takeover eliminating the chance to iterate and correct.
